source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: Front Matter: List of Terms and Introduction

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode, sides field says mirrored/same; glossary definitions in this chapter are treated as shared primitives other chapters will reuse

candidates.name: TrendBarByBody
candidates.quote: A bar with a body, which means that the close was above or below the open, indicating that there is at least a minor price movement.
candidates.description: Literal glossary test for a trend bar: the bar has any nonzero body (close != open). Weaker than a body-fraction test; kept because it is Brooks's own minimal definition, distinct from a 'most of the range' body-fraction reading.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (bar classification used as a signal-bar test)

complexity.reason: single-bar comparison of open and close

notes: The book elsewhere (and other chapters) use a body-fraction version of this same idea; this is the literal 'has any body at all' reading.

candidates.name: DojiBar
candidates.quote: A candle with a small body or no body at all.
candidates.description: A doji is the complement of a trend bar: its body is at most a small fraction of the bar's range (or of a fixed tick count on lower time frames). Neither side controls the bar.

complexity.reason: bare arithmetic on one bar, but the threshold is a judgment call Brooks does not number precisely

notes: Brooks gives tick examples ('one or two ticks on a 5 minute chart') rather than a fraction; 0.1 is a reading of 'small or no body'.

candidates.name: InsideBarInclusive
candidates.quote: A bar with a high that is at or below the high of the prior bar and a low that is at or above the low of the prior bar.
candidates.description: Inside bar test using Brooks's inclusive (at-or-beyond) boundary wording rather than strict inequality.

complexity.reason: single comparison of fixed-offset highs and lows

notes: Catalog's InsideBar uses strict > / < (high[N+1] > high[N] && low[N+1] < low[N]); Brooks's own wording is inclusive (<=, >=), so this is a near-duplicate with a boundary difference worth flagging to the authoring pass.

candidates.name: TripleInsideBars
candidates.quote: iii Three inside bars in a row, and a somewhat more reliable pattern than an ii.
candidates.description: Three consecutive inside bars: the current bar is inside the prior bar, which is itself inside the bar before it.
candidates.pseudocode: high[0] <= high[1] && low[0] >= low[1] && high[1] <= high[2] && low[1] >= low[2]

complexity.reason: chained inside-bar test over three fixed-offset bars

notes: 'ii' (two consecutive inside bars) is the same test as InsideBarInclusive applied once; not split out separately.

candidates.name: OutsideBarBrooks
candidates.quote: A bar with a high that is above or at the high of the prior bar and a low that is below the low of the prior bar.
candidates.description: Outside bar: the current bar's range engulfs the prior bar's range (inclusive on one side).

complexity.reason: single comparison of fixed-offset highs and lows

candidates.name: OutsideBarDirectional
candidates.quote: An outside bar with a close above its open.
candidates.description: An outside up bar (long) is an outside bar that also closes above its open; an outside down bar (short) closes below its open.
candidates.pseudocode: high[0] >= high[1] && low[0] <= low[1] && close[0] > open[0]
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (bar classification, often used as an entry or signal bar)

complexity.reason: outside-bar test plus a close/open comparison

candidates.name: InsideOutsideInside
candidates.quote: Inside-outside-inside—three consecutive bars where the second bar is an outside bar, and the third bar is an inside bar.
candidates.description: ioi pattern: the middle of three consecutive bars is an outside bar relative to the first, and the last bar is an inside bar relative to the middle bar. A breakout-mode setup.
candidates.pseudocode: high[1] >= high[2] && low[1] <= low[2] && high[0] <= high[1] && low[0] >= low[1]
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (breakout-mode setup, trade above/below the inside bar)

complexity.reason: chained inside/outside tests over three fixed-offset bars

candidates.name: OutsideOutside
candidates.quote: Outside-outside, an outside bar followed by a larger outside bar.
candidates.description: oo pattern: the prior bar is an outside bar, and the current bar is an outside bar relative to it whose range is larger than the prior bar's range.
candidates.pseudocode: high[1] >= high[2] && low[1] <= low[2] && high[0] >= high[1] && low[0] <= low[1] && (high[0] - low[0]) > (high[1] - low[1])

complexity.reason: chained outside-bar tests plus a range-size comparison

candidates.name: OutsideInsideOutside
candidates.quote: Outside-inside-outside, an outside bar followed by an inside bar, followed by an outside bar.
candidates.description: oio pattern over three consecutive bars: outside, then inside relative to it, then outside relative to that.
candidates.pseudocode: high[2] >= high[3] && low[2] <= low[3] && high[1] <= high[2] && low[1] >= low[2] && high[0] >= high[1] && low[0] <= low[1]

complexity.reason: chained inside/outside tests over four fixed-offset bars

candidates.name: SwingPoint
candidates.quote: A bar that looks like a spike up on the chart and extends up beyond the neighboring bars. Its high is at or above that of the bar before it and that of the bar after it.
candidates.description: A swing high/low is a one-bar fractal pivot confirmed one bar late: bar[1]'s high is at or above the highs of bar[2] and bar[0] (swing low is the mirror on lows). Foundational primitive for higher-high/lower-low, wedges, trend lines, and double tops/bottoms.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (structural pivot, confirmed one bar after it forms)

complexity.reason: a bare comparison of three fixed-offset bars, though its use elsewhere needs a persistent pivot history

notes: Central shared primitive; almost every swing-structure candidate below depends on it.

candidates.name: SwingExtendsPriorSwing
candidates.quote: A swing high that is higher than a previous swing high.
candidates.description: Higher high (long, trend continuation) / lower low (short): the most recent confirmed swing high/low exceeds the one before it.

complexity.reason: needs a persistent record of the last two confirmed swing pivots, not a fixed window

candidates.name: SwingRetracesAgainstPriorSwing
candidates.quote: A swing low that is higher than a previous swing low.
candidates.description: Higher low (long, pullback structure in an uptrend or a reversal-up signal) / lower high (short): the most recent confirmed swing low/high sits above/below the one before it, opposite the trending-extreme direction.

complexity.reason: needs a persistent record of the last two confirmed swing pivots

candidates.name: MovingAverageGapBar
candidates.quote: A bar that does not touch the moving average.
candidates.description: A gap bar's low sits above (bull) / high sits below (bear) the 20-bar EMA, i.e. the whole bar clears the moving average with a gap.

complexity.reason: requires an EMA series, not just fixed-offset price arithmetic

notes: The first pullback in a strong trend that produces one of these is called out by Brooks as often setting up a test of the trend's extreme; see V00-14 for the 20-in-a-row escalation.

candidates.name: TwentyMovingAverageGapBars
candidates.quote: Twenty or more consecutive bars that have not touched the moving average.
candidates.description: N or more consecutive moving-average gap bars (same side) is called out as a sign of a strong, persistent trend.

complexity.reason: a persistent counter of consecutive same-side gap bars, built on the EMA-gap primitive

candidates.name: MicroMeasuringGap
candidates.quote: If there is then a strong bull trend bar and the low of the bar after it is at or above the high of the bar before it, the midpoint between that low and that high is the micro measuring gap.
candidates.description: Around a strong trend bar, the bar after it does not overlap the bar before it at all (a true gap across the trend bar), a sign of strength and often a precursor to a measured move.

complexity.reason: cross-bar comparison spanning three bars, gated on a trend-bar classification of the middle bar

notes: Reused verbatim as a breakout-strength sign later in the chapter (pages 55, 57); one primitive, cited from both places.

candidates.name: SessionOpeningGap
candidates.quote: An opening gap is a common occurrence and is present if the open of the first bar of today is beyond the high or low of the prior bar (the last bar of yesterday) or of the entire day.
candidates.description: The first bar of a new session opens beyond the prior session's last bar's (or the whole prior day's) high/low.

complexity.reason: needs a session/date-boundary detection (first bar of the trading day), like the Date-series pattern used elsewhere in the corpus

candidates.name: GapReversalBar
candidates.quote: A formation in which the current bar extends one tick beyond the prior bar back into the gap.
candidates.description: After an opening gap, a subsequent bar trades one tick back into the gap (beyond the first bar's low for a gap-up open).
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry one tick into the gap, at the next bar's open once triggered

complexity.reason: depends on the opening-gap primitive plus a one-tick offset test

candidates.name: BarPullback
candidates.quote: In an upswing, a bar pullback is a bar with a low below the low of the prior bar.
candidates.description: The minimal one-bar pullback test: the current bar's low undercuts the prior bar's low in an upswing (mirrored for a downswing). Same idea is defined twice in the glossary under 'bar pullback' and 'pullback bar'.

complexity.reason: single comparison of fixed-offset lows

notes: Glossary defines this twice with the same meaning ('bar pullback' page 15, 'pullback bar' page 25); one candidate, both pages cited.

candidates.name: BreakoutBeyondPriorExtreme
candidates.quote: The high or low of the current bar extends beyond some prior price of significance such as a swing high or low, the high or low of any prior bar, a trend line, or a trend channel.
candidates.description: General breakout definition, simplified to the bar-of-significance case: the current bar's high/low exceeds a prior swing high/low or a fixed-lookback highest/lowest. The trend-line/channel forms of 'prior price of significance' are recorded separately (V00-33/34) since they need pivot and line projection.
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry one tick beyond the breakout bar

complexity.reason: 'prior price of significance' is Brooks's umbrella term for swing highs, any prior bar, or a trend line; a faithful version needs swing-pivot detection

candidates.name: BreakoutBarStrongBody
candidates.quote: A bar that creates a breakout. It is usually a strong trend bar.
candidates.description: A breakout bar is a breakout (V00-19) that is also a strong trend bar (large body, small tails). Kept as a named composite since Brooks treats the pairing as its own concept.
candidates.pseudocode: high[0] >= highest(high, lookback) && close[0] > open[0] && (close[0]-open[0]) >= bodyFraction*(high[0]-low[0])
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry one tick beyond the breakout bar

complexity.reason: inherits the swing/prior-bar ambiguity of the underlying breakout definition

candidates.name: BreakoutPullbackWindow
candidates.quote: A small pullback of one to about five bars that occurs within a few bars after a breakout.
candidates.description: A pullback that begins within a few bars of a breakout and lasts 1-5 bars is read as a with-trend setup expecting the breakout to resume, rather than a failed breakout.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context classification feeding a with-trend entry)

complexity.reason: needs persistent bar counters since the last breakout event and since the pullback began

candidates.name: BreakoutTestNearEntry
candidates.quote: A breakout pullback that comes close to the original entry price to test a breakeven stop.
candidates.description: Price returns to within a small tolerance of the position's entry price after a breakout, i.e. a test of a breakeven stop; may overshoot or undershoot by a few ticks.

complexity.reason: needs the live entry price and a tick-based tolerance, not just bar prices

candidates.name: FailedFailureResumption
candidates.quote: A failure that fails, resuming in the direction of the original breakout, and therefore a breakout pullback.
candidates.description: After a breakout fails (price reverses back through the breakout bar), a second failure of that failure resumes the original breakout direction, treated as more reliable because it is a second signal.
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry one tick beyond the re-breakout bar

complexity.reason: needs to track a breakout event, its failure, and a subsequent re-breakout across a variable-length window

candidates.name: FiveTickFailureReversal
candidates.quote: A trade in the Emini that reaches five ticks beyond the signal bar and then reverses.
candidates.description: A breakout that runs only N ticks beyond the signal bar's extreme before the next bar's opposite extreme falls back beyond it, an instrument-specific (Emini-tuned) small failed move often setting up a trade in the opposite direction.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context classification of a failed scalp attempt)

complexity.reason: needs the signal bar's extreme carried forward plus a tick-based offset, but is a fixed two-bar test once that state exists

notes: Brooks gives the tick count for the Emini specifically; treat as instrument-specific like CloseNearPriorLow's XX.

candidates.name: LedgeFlatExtreme
candidates.quote: A bull ledge is a small trading range with a bottom created by two or more bars with identical lows.
candidates.description: Two or more bars within a lookback window share (approximately) the same low, forming a flat floor (bull ledge) or, mirrored, the same high forming a flat ceiling (bear ledge).
candidates.pseudocode: countIf(abs(low[i] - low[j]) <= tolerance*tickSize, over pairs in lookback) >= 2

complexity.reason: a tolerance-based equality test over a small window of bars, with cross-bar bookkeeping

candidates.name: MicroDoubleExtreme
candidates.quote: Consecutive or nearly consecutive bars with lows that are near the same price.
candidates.description: A micro double bottom/top: two nearby bars (within a few bars of each other) have lows (or highs) within a small tolerance of each other, without needing full swing-pivot detection.

complexity.reason: tolerance-based near-equality over a short, variable lag

candidates.name: DoubleExtremeSwing
candidates.quote: A chart formation in which the low of the current bar is about the same as the low of a prior swing low.
candidates.description: Full double bottom/top: the current bar's low (high) is within tolerance of a prior confirmed swing low (high), which can be one bar or 20+ bars earlier.
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry one tick beyond the second low/high's signal bar

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection plus a tolerance test across a variable and potentially long lookback

candidates.name: DoubleExtremeFlagContext
candidates.quote: A pause or bull flag in a bull trend that has two spikes down to around the same price and then reverses back into a bull trend.
candidates.description: A double bottom/top that occurs as a with-trend flag (pause) rather than a standalone reversal pattern: the double extreme forms inside an established trend in the trend's own direction.
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry one tick beyond the second low/high's signal bar

complexity.reason: adds a trend-context gate on top of the already-hard double-extreme swing test

candidates.name: DoubleExtremePullbackSetup
candidates.quote: A buy setup composed of a double bottom followed by a deep pullback that forms a higher low.
candidates.description: A double bottom (top) followed by a deep pullback that itself forms a higher low (lower high), i.e. the double-extreme swing plus a subsequent higher-low/lower-high swing.
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry one tick beyond the higher-low/lower-high signal bar

complexity.reason: composite of two already-hard swing-structure primitives

candidates.name: ReversalBarMinimum
candidates.quote: The minimum that a bull reversal bar should have is either a close above its open (a bull body) or a close above its midpoint.
candidates.description: The floor test for a bull/bear reversal bar as a signal bar: the bar closes above its own open, or at least above its own midpoint, in the reversing direction. Central primitive for the whole reversals book.
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry one tick beyond the reversal (signal) bar

complexity.reason: single-bar arithmetic on open/high/low/close

notes: Also defined in the glossary under 'reversal bar' (page 22-23) with the same substance; cited from its most rule-like statement.

candidates.name: ReversalBarOpenNearPriorClose
candidates.quote: An open near or below the close of the prior bar and a close above the open and above the prior bar's close.
candidates.description: One quality marker of a strong bull reversal bar: it opens at or below the prior bar's close, then closes above both its own open and the prior close.
candidates.pseudocode: open[0] <= close[1] + tolerance*tickSize && close[0] > open[0] && close[0] > close[1]

complexity.reason: fixed-offset comparisons plus a small tick tolerance

candidates.name: ReversalBarTailFraction
candidates.quote: A lower tail that is about one-third to one-half the height of the bar and a small or nonexistent upper tail.
candidates.description: A strong bull reversal bar has a lower tail roughly a third to a half of the bar's total range, and little to no upper tail (mirrored for bear).

complexity.reason: single-bar arithmetic on open/high/low/close against fixed fractions

candidates.name: ReversalBarLowOverlapWithPrior
candidates.quote: Not much overlap with the prior bar or bars.
candidates.description: A strong reversal bar overlaps only a small fraction of its range with the prior N bars' ranges.

complexity.reason: needs an overlap-fraction computation across a small window, not a single fixed comparison

candidates.name: ReversalBarFollowThroughStrong
candidates.quote: The bar after the signal bar is not a doji inside bar and instead is a strong entry bar.
candidates.description: Quality marker read from the entry/follow-through bar itself (the bar after the signal bar): it should be a strong trend bar, not a doji inside bar. Useful for post-hoc scoring of a signal but not knowable before the entry bar closes.

complexity.reason: the condition is about the bar that would follow an entry decision, so using it live needs a design decision (e.g. score after the fact, or delay entry by a bar)

candidates.name: ReversalBarReversesMultipleBars
candidates.quote: A close that reverses (closes above) the closes and highs of more than one bar.
candidates.description: A strong reversal bar's close exceeds (bull) / undercuts (bear) the closes and highs/lows of more than one prior bar.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] > highest(high, reversedBars) && close[0] > highest(close, reversedBars)

complexity.reason: a small-window highest/average style loop rather than a single fixed comparison

candidates.name: TrendBarMajorityInDirection
candidates.quote: Most of the bars are trend bars in the direction of the trend.
candidates.description: Over a lookback window, most bars are trend bars closing in the trend's direction, a sign-of-strength context filter.
candidates.pseudocode: countIf(close[i] > open[i], i in 0..lookback-1) >= majorityFraction * lookback

complexity.reason: a counting loop over a window, gated on an already-assumed trend direction

candidates.name: MinimalBodyOverlapConsecutive
candidates.quote: There is very little overlap of the bodies of consecutive bars.
candidates.description: In a strong trend, the current bar's low sits at or just a tick or two below the prior bar's close (bull), showing little body overlap between consecutive bars.

complexity.reason: a single comparison against a tick-based tolerance

candidates.name: ShavedBodyBar
candidates.quote: A shaved top has no tail at the top and a shaved bottom has no tail at the bottom.
candidates.description: A bar with (approximately) no tail at one or both ends: for a bull bar, the close sits at or within a tick of the high (shaved top) or the open sits at or within a tick of the low (shaved bottom).

complexity.reason: single-bar arithmetic against a tick tolerance

candidates.name: BodyGapBetweenBars
candidates.quote: Occasionally, there are gaps between the bodies (for example, the open of a bar might be above the close of the prior bar in a bull trend).
candidates.description: The current bar's open trades beyond the prior bar's close in the trend direction, a body-to-body gap sign of strength.

complexity.reason: single comparison of fixed-offset open and close

notes: Same shape of test recurs almost verbatim as a breakout-spike sign of strength (page 57): 'One or more bars in the spike have an open that is above the close of the prior bar.' One primitive, cited from both places.

candidates.name: PullbackSizeThreshold
candidates.quote: There are small, infrequent, and mostly sideways pullbacks.
candidates.description: In a strong trend, pullbacks stay below a fixed size (points or a multiple of the recent range) - a context filter for trend strength.

complexity.reason: needs a running definition of 'the current pullback's range', which is cross-bar state, not a fixed window

notes: Brooks's example numbers (Emini average range ~12 points, pullbacks under 3-4 points) are instrument- and volatility-specific; an ATR-relative version may be more portable.

candidates.name: NoStraddleAcrossMovingAverage
candidates.quote: No two consecutive trend bar closes occur on the opposite side of the moving average.
candidates.description: In a strong trend, no two consecutive trend-bar closes straddle the EMA (one above, one below) - a context filter for trend strength.
candidates.pseudocode: !((close[0] > ema[0]) != (close[1] > ema[1]) && close[0] != open[0] && close[1] != open[1])

complexity.reason: requires the EMA series plus a two-bar comparison

candidates.name: VolumeSpikeOnBreakout
candidates.quote: If the volume of the large breakout bar is 10 to 20 times the average volume of recent bars, the chance of follow-through buying and a possible measured move increases.
candidates.description: The breakout bar's volume is a large multiple of its own recent average volume, a sign of strength gate.

complexity.reason: a window average compared against a large multiple, standard volume-filter shape

candidates.name: SpikeDurationNoPullback
candidates.quote: The spike grows to five to 10 bars without pulling back for more than a bar or so.
candidates.description: A trend spike runs for N bars with no pullback longer than one bar, a strength sign for the current move.

complexity.reason: needs persistent counters for the spike's length and the longest pullback within it

candidates.name: FollowThroughBarSizeAdequate
candidates.quote: The next two or three bars also have bull bodies that are at least the average size of the recent bull and bear bodies.
candidates.description: The bars following a breakout/reversal bar have bodies at least as large as the recent average body size, confirming follow-through.

complexity.reason: a window average of body sizes compared against the current bar's body

candidates.name: SpikeBarLowNearPriorClose
candidates.quote: One or more bars in the spike have a low that is at or just one tick below the close of the prior bar.
candidates.description: During a bull spike, a bar's low sits at or within one tick of the prior bar's close (eager buying with almost no giveback); mirrored for bear spikes on highs.

complexity.reason: single comparison against a tick tolerance

notes: Same shape of test as MinimalBodyOverlapConsecutive (V00-37); recorded separately because Brooks states it specifically for breakout/reversal spikes.

candidates.name: CloseNearBarExtreme
candidates.quote: One or more bars in the spike have a close on the bar's high or just one tick below its high.
candidates.description: A bar in a bull spike closes on or within a tick of its own high, showing urgency into the close.

complexity.reason: single-bar arithmetic against a tick tolerance, same shape as ShavedBodyBar

candidates.name: GrowingTrendBarDominanceInRange
candidates.quote: There is growing buying pressure in the trading range, represented by many large bull trend bars, and the bull trend bars are clearly more prominent than the bear trend bars in the range.
candidates.description: Over a lookback window inside a trading range, the sum (or count) of bull trend-bar bodies exceeds that of bear trend-bar bodies by a margin, ahead of a breakout.
candidates.pseudocode: sumIf(close[i]-open[i], close[i]>open[i], lookback) > dominanceMultiple * sumIf(open[i]-close[i], close[i]<open[i], lookback)

complexity.reason: a window-summation loop comparing two conditional sums

candidates.name: FirstPullbackDelayAfterBreakout
candidates.quote: The first pullback occurs only after three or more bars of breaking out.
candidates.description: The first pullback after a breakout does not begin until at least N bars have elapsed since the breakout bar, a strength sign.

complexity.reason: needs a persistent bar counter since the breakout event

candidates.name: FirstPullbackShortDuration
candidates.quote: The first pullback lasts only one or two bars, and it follows a bar that is not a strong bear reversal bar.
candidates.description: The first pullback after a breakout is short (1-2 bars) and does not begin with a strong opposite-direction reversal bar, a strength sign.

complexity.reason: needs a pullback-length counter plus a reversal-bar classification of the bar that started it

candidates.name: FirstPullbackNoBreakeven
candidates.quote: The first pullback does not reach the breakout point and does not hit a breakeven stop (the entry price).
candidates.description: The first pullback after a breakout does not retrace far enough to reach the breakout price / a breakeven stop, a strength sign.

complexity.reason: needs the live entry/breakout price and a tick tolerance

candidates.name: BreakoutReversesManyPriorBars
candidates.quote: This breakout bar has a high and close that are above the highs and closes of five or even 20 or more bars.
candidates.description: A breakout bar's close (and high) exceed the highs and closes of many prior bars (5 to 20+), a strength sign; the close-based version is stronger than the high-based version.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] > highest(close, reversedBars) && close[0] > highest(high, reversedBars)

complexity.reason: a highest-over-window comparison, standard shape

candidates.name: High1Leg
candidates.quote: In a sideways or downward move in a bull trend or a trading range, the first bar whose high is above the high of the prior bar is a high 1, and this ends the first leg of the sideways or down move.
candidates.description: High 1 (long) / low 1 (short): the first bar in a pullback whose high exceeds the prior bar's high (mirrored on lows), ending the first leg of the correction and forming a with-trend buy/sell setup.
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry one tick beyond the high 1 / low 1 bar

complexity.reason: needs a persistent leg counter reset at each swing-direction change, not a fixed-window test

notes: Foundational H1/L1 primitive for the whole 'bar counting' family described in the MINING brief.

candidates.name: High2Leg
candidates.quote: If the market does not turn into a bull swing and instead continues sideways or down, label the next occurrence of a bar with a high above the high of the prior bar as a high 2, ending the second leg.
candidates.description: High 2 (long) / low 2 (short): the second occurrence, after a high 1 fails to resume the trend, of a bar whose high exceeds the prior bar's high - the classic ABC-correction entry.
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry one tick beyond the high 2 / low 2 bar

complexity.reason: same persistent leg-counter state as High1Leg, one step further

candidates.name: High34WedgeLeg
candidates.quote: If the bull pullback ends after a third leg, the buy setup is a high 3 and is usually a type of wedge bull flag.
candidates.description: High 3 / high 4 (long) and low 3 / low 4 (short): third and fourth occurrences of the same high-above-prior-high (low-below-prior-low) test, usually forming a wedge-shaped pullback.
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry one tick beyond the high 3/4 or low 3/4 bar

complexity.reason: same persistent leg-counter state, extended further and overlapping with wedge/three-push pattern recognition

candidates.name: FailedFourthLegReversal
candidates.quote: If the low 4 fails (a bar extends above the high of the low 4 signal bar after the low 4 short is triggered), the price action indicates that the bears have lost control.
candidates.description: After a low 4 (high 4) short (long) setup triggers, if a subsequent bar breaks back above the low 4 signal bar's high (below the high 4 signal bar's low), the failed fourth-leg reading signals a possible control change and permits a reversal trade.
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry one tick beyond the failure bar

complexity.reason: depends on the already-hard leg-counting state plus tracking whether that specific setup triggered and then failed

candidates.name: WithTrendMajorityFilter
candidates.quote: If most of the past 10 or 20 bars are above the moving average, trend setups and trades are likely on the buy side.
candidates.description: A with-trend context gate: most of the last N bars closed above (long) / below (short) the 20-bar EMA.
candidates.pseudocode: countIf(close[i] > ema[i], i in 0..lookback-1) >= majorityFraction * lookback

complexity.reason: a counting loop against the EMA over a window

candidates.name: PullbackRetracement75Percent
candidates.quote: In general, the odds that a pullback will get back to the prior trend's extreme fall substantially if the pullback retraces 75 percent or more.
candidates.description: Once a pullback retraces 75% or more of the move it is correcting, treat it as more likely a new trend in the opposite direction than a pullback in the old one - a context-reclassification filter.

complexity.reason: needs identification of the trend's start and extreme, which requires swing/leg detection, not just fixed-offset prices

candidates.name: ClimaxOvershoot
candidates.quote: A move that has gone too far too fast and has now reversed direction to either a trading range or an opposite trend. Most climaxes end with trend channel overshoots and reversals.
candidates.description: A climax: an accelerated, overextended move that ends with an overshoot of its trend channel line and then reverses. The design decision is what counts as 'too far too fast' before coding a test.
candidates.pseudocode: n/a - design decision needed for 'too far too fast'

complexity.reason: the concept is real and heavily used in this book, but needs a design decision (rate-of-move threshold, channel-overshoot detection) before it can be coded at all

candidates.name: TrendChannelLineOvershoot
candidates.quote: One or more bars penetrating a trend channel line.
candidates.description: A bar's high (low) penetrates a rising (falling) trend channel line projected from recent swing highs (lows), often a climax/reversal sign.

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection and trend-channel-line projection from those pivots

candidates.name: TrendChannelLineUndershoot
candidates.quote: A bar approaches a trend channel line but the market reverses away from the line without reaching or penetrating it.
candidates.description: A bar approaches but does not reach a trend channel line before reversing away from it, the mirror case of an overshoot.

complexity.reason: needs the same trend-channel-line projection as the overshoot primitive

candidates.name: MicroChannelTightness
candidates.quote: A very tight channel where most of the bars have their highs and lows touching the trend line and, often, also the trend channel line.
candidates.description: A micro trend channel: most bars in a short lookback have their extremes essentially on both the trend line and the trend channel line (an extremely tight, low-pullback move).
candidates.pseudocode: countIf(abs(high[i] - trendChannelLine(i)) <= tolerance, lookback) >= majorityFraction * lookback

complexity.reason: needs trend-line and trend-channel-line projection plus a tolerance-based counting loop against both lines

candidates.name: WedgeThreePush
candidates.quote: Traditionally, a three-push move with each push extending further and the trend line and trend channel line at least minimally convergent, creating a rising or descending triangle with a wedge shape.
candidates.description: A wedge / three-push pattern: three successive swing extremes (each usually beyond the last) with a converging trend line and trend channel line, tradable as a reversal or as a with-trend flag.
candidates.pseudocode: swingCount(3) && each swing extends beyond the previous && trendLineSlope converges with trendChannelLineSlope
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry one tick beyond the breakout of the third push's opposite trend line

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection, leg counting across three pushes, and trend-line/trend-channel-line convergence

candidates.name: ShrinkingStairsMomentumWane
candidates.quote: It is a series of three or more trending highs in a bull trend or lows in a bear trend where each breakout to a new extreme is by fewer ticks than the prior breakout, indicating waning momentum.
candidates.description: Three or more successive trend-extending swings where each new extreme is reached by a smaller increment than the previous one, a momentum-fading context signal.
candidates.pseudocode: swingExtreme[0] - swingExtreme[1] < swingExtreme[1] - swingExtreme[2] && swingExtreme[1] - swingExtreme[2] > 0

complexity.reason: needs a persistent record of multiple successive swing pivots and their increment sizes

candidates.name: TrendFromOpen
candidates.quote: A trend that begins at the first or one of the first bars of the day and extends for many bars without a pullback, and the start of the trend remains as one of the extremes of the day for much if not all of the day.
candidates.description: The session's opening bar(s) begin a trend that runs many bars without a meaningful pullback, and the session open/first extreme stays the day's high or low for most of the session.

complexity.reason: needs session-boundary detection, a persistent no-pullback bar counter, and tracking the running session extreme

candidates.name: SecondSignalWithinFewBars
candidates.quote: The second time within a few bars of the first entry where there is an entry bar based on the same logic as the first entry.
candidates.description: A second occurrence, within a short window, of a setup that already fired once and failed, treated as more reliable than the first attempt (a 'second signal').
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry one tick beyond the second signal bar

complexity.reason: needs generic tracking of 'the same setup fired recently', which depends on whatever underlying pattern is being repeated

candidates.name: SecondMovingAverageGapBarSetup
candidates.quote: If there is a first moving average gap bar and a reversal toward the moving average does not reach the moving average, and instead the move away from the moving average continues, it is the next reversal in the direction of the moving average.
candidates.description: After a first moving-average gap bar, if the following pullback toward the EMA fails to reach it and the trend resumes, the next EMA-gap-bar reversal setup is a 'second' setup with the same logic.
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry one tick beyond the setup bar

complexity.reason: needs to remember a prior gap-bar event and whether the subsequent pullback reached the EMA, cross-bar state beyond a simple counter

candidates.name: BreakoutPullbackFailedBreakout
candidates.quote: If instead you thought that the breakout would fail, you would not use the term pullback and instead would see the pullback as a failed breakout.
candidates.description: The same post-breakout pullback is read as a breakout pullback (with-trend, resumption expected) or a failed breakout (reversal expected), a labeling distinction that hinges on whether the pullback exceeds the breakout point - i.e. this is the negation gate between V00-21 (breakout pullback) and a reversal read of the same price action.

complexity.reason: needs the breakout event's price level carried forward, then a single comparison against it

notes: Definitional complement to BreakoutPullbackWindow (V00-21): same price action, opposite label, depending on whether the breakout point is exceeded.

rejected.quote: Traders who buy as a bull signal bar is forming rather than waiting for it to close and then entering on a buy stop at one tick above its high.
rejected.reason: early longs/shorts require entering before the signal bar closes, i.e. tick-level data inside the bar, which the engine does not have.

rejected.quote: A sell-off in a bear spike or a tight bear channel without significant pullbacks and that extends further than the fundamentals would dictate.
rejected.reason: meltdown/melt-up require judging what fundamentals would dictate, data the engine cannot have.

rejected.quote: As the first bar of the breakout bar is forming, it spends most of its time near its high and the pullbacks are small.
rejected.reason: requires intrabar tick-level path information, not just the bar's OHLC.

rejected.quote: There is a sense of urgency. You find yourself waiting through countless bars for a good with-trend pullback and one never comes, yet the market slowly continues to trend.
rejected.reason: pure trader psychology/discretion with no independent bar-level test; the surrounding mechanical signs of strength are captured separately.

rejected.quote: The overall context makes a breakout likely, like the resumption of a trend after a pullback, or a higher low or lower low test of the bear low after a strong break above the bear trend line.
rejected.reason: circular discretionary context judgment ('likely because it looks likely') with no independent bar-level test beyond primitives already captured elsewhere.

rejected.quote: Some traders use simple game theory and increase the size of a trade after one or more losing trades (this is called a martingale approach to trading).
rejected.reason: a position-sizing scheme, not a bar-level entry/exit condition; the book itself argues it does not work in practice.

rejected.quote: Only look at the chart and it will tell you what you need to know.
rejected.reason: the surrounding discussion explicitly rejects news, TV pundits, and other traders' opinions as trading inputs -- data the engine does not have and should not use.

chapter_summary: This chapter is the book's front matter: the List of Terms glossary (pages 13-28) and the Introduction (pages 29-62), including the 'Signs of Strength' bullet lists and the H1/H2/H3/H4, L1/L2/L3/L4 bar-counting basics. Almost none of it is chart-example commentary; instead it is unusually dense with precise mechanical primitives (reversal bar minimum, swing high/low, inside/outside bar, moving-average gap bar, trend/doji bar, breakout, ledge, micro double top/bottom, wedge/three-push) that other Brooks chapters will reuse constantly -- define these once and reference by id rather than re-deriving. The bar-counting family (V00-52..56) and swing-structure family (V00-10..12, 63) are the two richest but hardest veins; almost every later reversal-pattern chapter will depend on them. The philosophical middle of the Introduction (institutions, gambling, news, indicators) yielded almost nothing mechanical and is reflected mainly in the rejected list.
